pr_title: Throw if a component produces an invalid render tree. Fixes #24579
pr_body:
The cause of #24579 was what I thought. Components aren't allowed to produce invalid trees - this has always been an unsupported situation. However it's unfortunate that developers can produce invalid trees using something as reasonable-seeming as a `try`/`catch` block, so we need to do something to prevent this class of problems.

Previously we didn't detect this scenario, so the diffing logic could just get stuck on it. With this PR we check whether there were any unclosed tree entries left behind, and if so, fails the entire rendering process with an exception, so the behavior is properly defined.

Longer term we might want to prevent the `try`/`catch` block at compile time in the Razor compiler, but this runtime check is still desirable, and is sufficient to block the situation.

issue_context.title: Try / Catch does not work in razor markup
issue_context.body:
### Describe the bug Try/Catch does not work in razor code when encountering index out of bounds. Expected behavior of code below would be to see "Index out of bounds" in the div. Actual behavior, page hangs and eventually gives out of memory exception. ### To Reproduce Create standard Blazor WASM project. Replace Counter page with following: ```razor @page "/counter" @try {
@Strings[5]
} catch (Exception ex) {
@ex.ToString()
} @code { private List Strings = new List { "String one", "String 2" }; } ``` ### Exceptions (if any) Out of Memory error ### Further technical details .NET Core SDK (reflecting any global.json): Version: 3.1.302 Commit: 41faccf259 Runtime Environment: OS Name: Windows OS Version: 10.0.18363 OS Platform: Windows RID: win10-x64 Base Path: C:\Program Files\dotnet\sdk\3.1.302\ Host (useful for support): Version: 3.1.6 Commit: 3acd9b0cd1 .NET Core SDKs installed: 3.1.300 [C:\Program Files\dotnet\sdk] 3.1.302 [C:\Program Files\dotnet\sdk] .NET Core runtimes installed: Microsoft.AspNetCore.All 2.1.20 [C:\Program Files\dotnet\shared\Microsoft.AspNetCore.All] Microsoft.AspNetCore.App 2.1.20 [C:\Program Files\dotnet\shared\Microsoft.AspNetCore.App] Microsoft.AspNetCore.App 3.1.4 [C:\Program Files\dotnet\shared\Microsoft.AspNetCore.App] Microsoft.AspNetCore.App 3.1.6 [C:\Program Files\dotnet\shared\Microsoft.AspNetCore.App] Microsoft.NETCore.App 2.1.20 [C:\Program Files\dotnet\shared\Microsoft.NETCore.App] Microsoft.NETCore.App 3.1.4 [C:\Program Files\dotnet\shared\Microsoft.NETCore.App] Microsoft.NETCore.App 3.1.6 [C:\Program Files\dotnet\shared\Microsoft.NETCore.App] Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App 3.1.4 [C:\Program Files\dotnet\shared\Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App] Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App 3.1.6 [C:\Program Files\dotnet\shared\Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App] - Visual Studio 2019 16.6.5
comments:
Resolved in https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/24650

@kevonh Using try/catch during rendering logic can result in corrupted output which caused this behavior. The way we're fixing it via #24650 is to detect this situation and throw, instead of having the undefined behavior you observed.

The reason try/catch is problematic during rendering is because it's like other situations where you emit output. Once you emitted it, you can't take it back. If your `try` branch already starts outputting some elements but never closes them because execution moves on to a `catch` block that supresses the exception, then the output has unbalanced tags which is an invalid document.

So the overall pattern application developers need to follow is putting any possibly-throwing logic into the component's `@code` block (e.g., lifecycle methods, event handlers, etc.). We have a different issue on the backlog (#13452) that would provide mechanisms for recovery from per-component exceptions, including during the rendering logic, but that's not in scope for this fix.

review_comments: Is it always guaranteed that the index is going to be in range (assuming there are no bugs in the RenderTreeBuilder code) I believe that's the case, but given we are dealing with "failure modes" here I ask just in case to be more cautious.
Yes, but even if not, the code here is certain to throw (either from the `throw` statement on L695, or an index-out-of-range on L694), which is all we need.

Do we have validation for when the close statements balance out but are in different order? For example
```
builder.OpenElement()
builder.OpenRegion().
builder.CloseElement();
builder.CloseRegion()
```

It's a good point to raise, but I think we're OK with this one. In practice all of the `Close` methods will close whatever frame is outstanding on the stack, so even if you do deliberately get the order wrong it won't be harmful. The only weirdness you could cause by this would be failing to pass parameters to a child component because that's the only difference between the close methods.

Considering how perf-critical is this low-level part of rendering, we wouldn't want penalize people using `.razor` to produce normal components by introducing extra checking logic for cases that a valid `.razor` component could never trigger. We've always been clear that anyone writing rendertreebuilder logic manually is in the same situation as people writing C# logic manually: if you write a bug, you have a bug.
